title: What would bring life back to high streets?
label: 17 November 2026 · High streets and local businesses
summary: The committee heard that rising costs, empty properties and limited council capacity are making it hard to revive high streets. Retail and hospitality witnesses called for help with business costs and more support for local plans. Tax experts disagreed over whether cutting business rates helps tenants or mainly benefits landlords, and whether taxing online sales would help shops. Across both panels, witnesses stressed that tax changes alone can't give every town centre a workable future.

speakers.label: Aditi Sriram
speakers.name: Aditi Sriram
speakers.role: Economist, Institute for Public Policy Research

speakers.label: Professor Travers
speakers.name: Professor Tony Travers
speakers.role: Interim Dean, LSE School of Public Policy

glossary.definition: A tax generally charged to businesses occupying properties such as shops, pubs and warehouses.
A reassessment of a property's rental value, used to calculate its business rates bill.
A tax paid on earnings by workers and, separately, by their employers.
Value added tax, which is added to the price of many goods and services.
A reduction in the business rates bill for a property that meets specified conditions.
A government programme that provides funding for neighbourhood improvements shaped by local plans.
A process allowing councils to arrange leases for some long-empty commercial properties.
Regional bodies led by elected mayors that carry out functions across several council areas.
Buying something online and picking it up from a shop or other collection point.

chapters.title: The costs of staying open
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses said several rising costs had hit shops and hospitality businesses at once, with particular concern about jobs for young people.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What has the April 2026 reassessment of property values meant for shops, pubs and other hospitality businesses?

evidence.quote: What is the impact of the April 2026 business rates revaluation on retail and businesses in the hospitality and leisure sector? What are you seeing?

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: For hospitality, it's been catastrophic. Pubs' assessed values rose by 76% on average and hotels' by 115%. The further 20% discount announced for pubs, clubs and live music venues helps, but it isn't enough.

evidence.quote: In a nutshell, it is catastrophic. I am talking specifically about hospitality. Since the revaluation, pubs on average went up 76%. Hotels on average have gone up 115%. It is completely untenable.
the PM announced a further 20% discounts for pubs, clubs and live music venues, which is helpful. It is certainly not enough

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: Retailers faced several changes together: new property values, the removal of earlier relief and changes to the rates charged. Even after the new lower rates for some properties, we estimate retailers' bills rose by about £1.1 billion. Those repeated changes make planning difficult.

evidence.quote: We had the impact of the valuation. We had the removal of the RHL—the retail, hospitality and leisure—so some of the covid reliefs that had been in place that had been slowly removed. Then we had the introduction of new and lower multipliers for retail and hospitality businesses
retailers still ended up paying more business rates on the back of the April 2026 valuation, to the tune of about £1.1 billion.
the fact that we have this up and down on an ongoing basis makes it very difficult for businesses to plan.

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: Higher employer national insurance has added to the pressure. More than 100,000 hospitality jobs have gone, and I say most were held by 18 to 24-year-olds. I support paying people more through the minimum wage, but businesses have also faced higher energy bills and rates. The timing matters.

evidence.quote: Since then, in hospitality, in my sector, we have lost north of 100,000 jobs. When you dig down into the minutiae of that, the vast majority were jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds.

We have business rates, the utility bills that you just mentioned, the NI increase, and now they are saddled with a minimum wage increase, so I wonder whether the time was right. Ultimately, I support the minimum wage increase.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: You say the proposed national insurance change could save about £750 per young employee. Many local pubs don't employ 20 people. Would that really be enough to keep them going?

evidence.quote: You said that if you were to employ 20 young people that would save you £15,000 a year.

My father had one of the largest pubs in our town and did not employ anywhere near that amount. Do you think that it needs to go further than £750 an employee to really make a difference to most local pubs?

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: It's a start, especially alongside the rates discount. If I could choose the biggest change, though, I'd cut VAT for hospitality. Ours is 20%; in much of Europe, it's around 9% or 10%.

evidence.quote: It is certainly a start. You combine that with, as I said, the 20% reduction on business rates that was announced on day 3. All these small things add up to a decent amount of help.
No. 1 would be a VAT reduction. Bring us in line with the rest of Europe. We are 20%. Most of Europe is between 9% and 10%.

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: Retail has lost about 120,000 jobs too. Higher wages matter for workers, but employers have struggled to absorb repeated increases alongside national insurance. Raising the earnings level at which employers start paying that tax could make part-time, entry-level jobs more affordable. I hope the government acts quickly, though the review says to do so when public finances allow.

evidence.quote: Our number of job losses is about 120,000, so similar to what Sacha is saying.

while I think everybody accepts that it absolutely should go up, because it needs to in the context of the cost of living, we have seen above-inflationary increases on a sustained basis. That has been quite difficult for businesses to absorb, particularly when it was taken on top of the national insurance rise
Focusing on taking the threshold back up makes those local, entry-level, sometimes part-time—so people can manage around their studies—jobs much more economically viable
we really hope that the Government pick up that bit of it and implement it as quickly as possible. I appreciate that it says “when fiscal conditions allow”

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: Small independent shops and cafés particularly need support. They give a high street its character.

evidence.quote: For me, it is the independents. We are talking about the high street here. There is certainly a place for the big chains.

If we want to re-energise the high streets and give the high streets the personality, for me it is those family-run coffee shops, those family-run bakers or the small independent restaurants. They are the ones that need the support.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: The smallest employers can be largely protected from the national insurance rise. Their bigger worries include rent and soaring commercial energy bills. A tenant on a short lease may not have the money—or own the building—to make it cheaper to heat. That leaves little spare cash to maintain the shopfront, even if the council improves the street outside.

evidence.quote: if you are a very small employer you have a buffer that largely keeps you protected from the rises that we experienced if you have only a handful of employees. They are much more concerned with the cost of rent, the ownership mix that is on the high street and, most critically, energy bills.
you do not have the capital available to you to retrofit your property. You probably do not even own it. You are probably on a short lease.
People do not have the surpluses required to look after their properties in the way that they did. On the one hand, you might have a local authority that invests millions into redoing your pavements

chapters.title: Who benefits from lower rates?
chapters.takeaway: The first panel disagreed about how much rates relief reaches tenants and argued that rents, ownership and empty buildings also need attention.

turns.speaker: Chris Curtis
turns.text: If a shop's business rates bill falls, couldn't its landlord eventually charge more rent and take much of the benefit? Would another form of support help businesses more?

evidence.quote: most of that money that is cut in that tax relief ends up being swallowed up in the long run by higher rents in most places.
is it not better or more efficient to give support to the retail, hospitality and leisure industries through other reliefs in other places, maybe on national insurance

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: I don't accept that as a useful account of what happens in practice. Rents don't adjust instantly, and some landlords won't lower them to fill a vacant shop because of their lending arrangements. We wouldn't have one in seven properties empty if the market corrected itself that neatly. The underlying problem is that the total business rates burden is too high.

evidence.quote: No, I do not accept the argument. I am sure that, academically speaking, it probably is true. The reality of the situation though is that we do not have a perfect market that corrects itself minute by minute.
landlords who are not necessarily prepared to reduce their rent to get a vacant property occupied because it will have implications for their covenants on their lending.
We would not be sitting with one in seven properties across the country empty if that was true.
The reason why we are even having that debate is that the business rates burden is too high.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: I've seen people looking for premises while shops stand empty. The costs and complexity of taking on a property help explain that mismatch. Someone wanting to open a bookshop or bakery shouldn't have to become an expert in a complicated tax system.

evidence.quote: There are lots of other complexities that make it quite difficult for somebody who just has a passion—I want to open a bookshop, a coffee shop, or an independent baker—to now suddenly have to become an expert in this quite complicated tax system.
we have high vacancy rates on the high street and town centres, but also high demand for property, which exists and is a paradox.

turns.speaker: Mr Brash
turns.text: In places with limited spending power, I'm struck by the rents landlords still ask for. Should government do more about landlords leaving properties empty?

evidence.quote: I am stunned by some of the rent levels that are expected to be paid in an area of relative deprivation. Do the Government need to get more of a handle on this?
that is keeping these properties oftentimes empty for no good reason.

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: I'd like to see small businesses encouraged into boarded-up units. Altrincham shows what can happen: after a food court opened in its old market, independent businesses followed, and the council later made changes to the streets.

evidence.quote: I would love to see the Government encouraging smaller, almost cottage, businesses to go in there and create a bit of activity on the high street.
Someone who had an idea regarding hospitality opened up a food court in the old market, which was a huge success overnight. On the back of that, smaller independents started to open around that.
The council then jumped on board. It was like, “This is great. Look what they are doing”. They started to pedestrianise streets.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: I'd like more businesses to own their premises rather than spend so much of what they earn on rent. We could also let more organisations that permanently commit their assets to community purposes get automatic business rates relief, as charities do.

evidence.quote: We need to see more owner-operators.
so much of the surplus that you generate in a business goes towards paying your rent.

Anything with an asset lock, for example, should be within the scope. That is community benefit societies that are not charities and CICs. They could all be brought within the scope of automatic business rates relief, like the charities.

turns.speaker: Chris Curtis
turns.text: There's another problem: improving a shop can raise its assessed value and therefore its tax bill. How could we avoid discouraging improvements?

evidence.quote: if you invest in upgrading your store, that will pay higher business rates as a consequence. Are there any ideas on how we can stop that disincentive?

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: Don't raise the assessed value used for business rates just because someone improved an existing property.

evidence.quote: Do not increase the rate on the back of the higher valuation if it is an improvement. That is the problem, is it not? Anything that is improving an existing property should not increase the valuation that is used for business rates.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: Small grants for shopfronts can help too. In Birkenhead, we used public funding for modest improvements. Residents involved in Pride in Place keep raising derelict buildings: even scattered empty, neglected properties affect how people feel about their area.

evidence.quote: In Birkenhead, we used UKSPF money to do very light-touch shopfront improvements

Right out on top is dereliction, particularly in northern towns or post-industrial towns across the country. Dereliction is a massive factor when it comes to people not feeling proud about where they live.
It is this pepper-potting of vacancy and dereliction that brings down the way people feel about an area

chapters.title: Turning a high street plan into change
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses welcomed national attention to high streets but said towns need different plans, practical expertise and enough people to carry them out.

turns.speaker: Alan Strickland
turns.text: Some town centres in my area have very high vacancy rates. What would a response to those wider problems look like, beyond one change to tax or rent?

evidence.quote: my local town centre in Newton Aycliffe has a 26% vacancy rate. In Bishop Auckland it is one in three. Peterlee has a 40% vacancy rate.
What does a good systemic response to that look like?

turns.speaker: Caireen Wackett
turns.text: There's no single plan that works everywhere. The government's high street strategy recognises that different towns have different needs, and it's good that money is available. The harder step is helping councils and local people turn that into a plan they can carry out, then learn what works.

evidence.quote: There is not one blueprint. Unfortunately, there is not one thing to do that is going to better the state of our high streets.

The money that has been allocated is amazing. There definitely was not any money back in 2011. There are now funds, but it is about how that is deployed, how we are testing and learning, and how we are highlighting best practice
Taking it into an action plan is the biggest challenge.

turns.speaker: Caireen Wackett
turns.text: Councils need help first to understand their own town and hear from the people involved, then to decide what to do over time. They also need ways to judge social benefits, not just immediate financial returns. Otherwise, it's tempting to choose a visible pavement project over a smaller change that may matter more in the long run.

evidence.quote: we do not do anything until we audit and understand the situation, consult with all the stakeholders and imagine what the vision and the answer could be. We then think about a roadmap and application over time.
it is easy to focus on the financial return of something as opposed to the broader economic and social returns.
You tend to lean into the things that are more optically there, such as, “Let’s repave a pavement”, as opposed to doing the smaller, more meaningful, maybe longer‑term, more impactful changes.

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: Some councils have funding but don't know where to start. They need access to people who can help analyse their particular town and make decisions. Mayoral authorities could be places where that expertise sits and is shared with councils.

evidence.quote: there was Pride in Place money and high street fund money available, and yet the local authority did not know where to start or how to think about it.
there has to be a way to get that expertise down into the local level to the people who need to make the decisions.
They actually could be where those centres of excellence might sit. Then they can support their local authorities in their mayoral authorities.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: Good policy can still fail if a council lacks staff or expertise. We tried to work with Wirral Council on high street rental auctions, which could bring long-empty shops back into use. It was interested, but couldn't take the work further, even with a grant. Councils need somewhere to borrow specialist help.

evidence.quote: We tried to do a high street rental auction programme with it. There was a will and an interest in it, and it came from the community, not the council, but it did not have the capacity to take it any further.
Despite the fact that it wanted to do it and was interested, it just could not, even with the grant that came from MHCLG. It was just too much administrative burden
Good policy will sometimes land on a local authority that does not have the capacity, will or expertise

turns.speaker: Mr Brash
turns.text: Hartlepool has a very large shopping centre for its population, alongside supermarkets, out-of-town shopping and high streets. It can't sustain all of that unchanged. Who can help a place make the difficult decisions if its council lacks the capacity?

evidence.quote: Hartlepool has the third-largest covered shopping centre in the north of England and a population of 90,000. It cannot possibly sustain that. Added to that, it has all the various supermarkets with their free parking, several retail areas on the outskirts of town, and high streets.
Local authorities cannot do it. I am not convinced that combined authorities have the capacity. I am really interested in who else can.

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: The private sector has a role, but I don't know how to bring businesses together locally in every town. Retailers still value physical shops and face-to-face contact, even though most now sell online too.

evidence.quote: I do not know the answer to that. The private sector definitely has a role.

the vast majority of retailers realise the importance of physical space, locality, connection to customers and that face-to-face interaction. The vast majority of retailers are now selling digitally as well as physically.
As for how you create forums for them to come together locally in every single place across the country, I do not know.

turns.speaker: Caireen Wackett
turns.text: High streets need to be more than shopping areas: they can also have public services, places to learn and places for people to meet. That means bringing more organisations into each town's plans, which makes the job more complicated.

evidence.quote: We need our high streets to be public services, learning destinations and community social spaces.
it is no longer just the retail shopping space
That means that the complexity is even greater with the number of stakeholders that we have to pull around a table to help set the right vision.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: People leading change locally need time and support to visit places that have succeeded and understand how they did it. A written set of instructions won't be enough. Local authorities also need to trust those people and share some responsibility with them.

evidence.quote: It is not a toolkit. We do not research it and create a little toolkit for somebody to implement. It has to be experienced. We have to go there. We have to see it.
there needs to be a greater increase of trust within local ecosystems to find those place leaders and invest in them
We need local authorities to be a little more generous in giving away some of that responsibility and power.

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: Places need plans that fit them. Events can bring in visitors who spend money locally: Parklife brought about £13 million into the local economy. But whether that helps a particular town depends on the place.

evidence.quote: It has to be bespoke. You are right: there is not a toolbox. I do not know the geography of Hartlepool, so apologies.
It used to bring about £13 million into the local economy, whether it is hotels, bars, restaurants or taxis.
bringing more people in for a reason would.

turns.speaker: Mr Mohindra
turns.text: The discount for pubs, social clubs and live music venues didn't include nightclubs. What do you make of that?

evidence.quote: Do you want to comment on the fact that nightclubs were not included?

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: I was disappointed; I initially thought ‘clubs’ included nightclubs. I'll keep pushing on that. Small live music venues also need protecting: they're where artists can start out before reaching much larger audiences.

evidence.quote: when he said clubs I thought it meant nightclubs. It did not. It meant working men’s clubs and that kind of thing. I was slightly disappointed and the sector was as well. I do not understand why and it is something that I will be pushing further.
Stormzy did not become a huge pop star overnight. Stormzy started in those small live music venues. We need to protect this culture.

chapters.title: A tax designed for property, not profits
chapters.takeaway: The second panel challenged the focus on rates relief and proposed different reforms, while warning that tax alone won't fix struggling high streets.

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: I think the debate starts from a mistake. Over time, a cut in business rates mostly shows up as higher rent, so landlords receive much of the benefit. In my view, focusing on rates cuts to help shops is an expensive error.

evidence.quote: All the theory and evidence is that, in the long run, business rates are mostly capitalised into rent. If business rates are cut, in the long term that is a tax cut for landlords.
All the focus on reducing business rates is an error. It is an expensive policy error.

turns.speaker: Chris Curtis
turns.text: Helen Dickinson argued that rents don't adjust neatly and that tenants can benefit from relief. Does that persuade you?

evidence.quote: Helen in the previous panel—I do not know whether you heard it—made a persuasive argument that the market is so inefficient for these rental properties on high streets that actually a lot of it ends up going to the tenant. Do you think that that is persuasive?

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: Not without evidence. Tenants can compare properties and landlords can seek different tenants. It isn't clear to me why this rental market would work so differently.

evidence.quote: What is the evidence for it? Why should a rental market be inefficient in that way? It is really not clear that it should.
When someone is looking to rent premises, they look at different premises and different landlords. Landlords attract a variety of different potential tenants.

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: I'd make landlords responsible for paying business rates, stop improvements from increasing the assessed value, and reassess property values more often. Making landlords pay would mainly clarify who bears the cost in the long run, not magically remove it from tenants. The change should happen when a lease is granted or reviewed.

evidence.quote: The first thing I would do is to make it the landlord who pays, not the tenant. This would have only a limited practical impact, because ultimately that is what happens now
The second thing I would do is to exclude improvement from business rates valuations.
The final thing I would do is to have more regular revaluations.
The shift to making it a landlord’s liability would have to be on the next time a lease is granted or reviewed
In principle, the tenant should end up in the same place they are today.

turns.speaker: Professor Travers
turns.text: The system already has many different discounts and tax rates, which councils must account for. Every new exception also creates a boundary: one business qualifies while a similar one doesn't.

evidence.quote: There are huge numbers of reliefs and they require an enormous amount of accounting.
We not only have lots of reliefs, but we have different levels of multiplier.
there is always somebody just above the threshold who does not get the relief. Why is that particular line fair?

turns.speaker: Aditi Sriram
turns.text: The tax shouldn't discourage a business from improving its premises or expanding. One question is whether businesses should be taxed more according to profits than property. But councils rely on the relatively steady income from rates; profit-based taxes would fall more sharply in a downturn.

evidence.quote: We want to tax in a way that does not distort investment.
the small business rates relief, above which it might prevent small businesses expanding
It is based more on business profits rather than on property.
When we move towards profits, it is hit a lot more by downturns. Those are the two most important questions to answer in terms of rates.

turns.speaker: Professor Travers
turns.text: I'm not convinced rates are the main cause of high street decline. Some struggling places have many shops paying no rates, while other places with little relief have thriving high streets. Cars, out-of-town shopping and online retail have also changed where people shop.

evidence.quote: I am not 100% sure that business rates are the problem.

a very large proportion of all businesses on high streets pay no rates and they are in trouble. There are other places, notably London, where virtually no businesses get relief, or a small proportion of businesses get relief, and high streets are thriving.
There are more cars, more out-of-town retail and more online retail.

turns.speaker: Aditi Sriram
turns.text: Tax is too blunt a tool to remake a high street. Councils also need the money and staff to shape which businesses and services are there. Changing the tax treatment of vape shops, for example, isn't the same as planning a town centre people want to use.

evidence.quote: the tax system is an incredibly blunt policy instrument and cannot really fix our high streets.
It is less the tax system that has to deal with that and more local government and councils that need the capacity to choose who is on the high street and shape their high streets.
That involves not just the regulatory or planning permissions, but also the financial capacity within councils to do that work

turns.speaker: Professor Travers
turns.text: And if unwanted shops disappeared, that wouldn't necessarily mean other businesses were ready to move into their premises.

evidence.quote: if all the vape shops, betting shops and chicken shops disappeared, the question is, “Would there then be entrepreneurs waiting to move into those businesses?” I doubt that there are.

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: The present rules can even reward a landlord for letting an empty property to a tenant they suspect won't pay rates: the landlord is no longer responsible for the empty property's bill. Making landlords responsible would give them a stronger reason to check who they're renting to.

evidence.quote: It can be good business for a landlord to let an empty property to someone who he suspects is not going to pay rates because then the property is no longer empty and the landlord will not have the liability.
You would need to put liability on the landlord to change it. That is the way to stop the criminal businesses.

chapters.title: Letting regions keep more tax
chapters.takeaway: Regional control over tax income could reward growth, but witnesses debated how to protect places whose economies grow more slowly.

turns.speaker: Mr Brash
turns.text: If mayoral areas keep more of the business rates raised locally, won't richer places gain while areas already struggling fall further behind?

evidence.quote: The Government are putting forward proposals to allow mayoral areas to retain business rates. That is going to create winners and losers in all of this, and I am afraid that the losers are going to be areas that are already struggling.
The threat is that, 10 years hence, richer areas will be richer, and poorer areas will be poorer, is it not?

turns.speaker: Professor Travers
turns.text: The proposal is intended to leave areas no better or worse off when it starts: local tax income would replace grants they currently get. After that, faster-growing places would keep some of the extra revenue, which is the incentive. The government has proposed some protection for slower-growing areas, but not complete protection; the details aren't settled.

evidence.quote: I am assuming, from what they have said, that it will be neutral at the point of change, so nobody will be better or worse off at the point of change.
faster-growing regions will have to keep some of the uplift in the growth of the tax base. Otherwise, it would not be an incentive.
MHCLG has said that there will be tapers on growth and protection for losers, but they are not complete.
We do not know how that will all land yet

turns.speaker: Mr Brash
turns.text: Should mayors also be able to cut local business rates to attract companies to areas struggling to secure private investment?

evidence.quote: Is there an argument to go further and give local mayoral authorities the power to cut tax, to reduce the multipliers and to incentivise the crowding in of companies’ investment into an area that is struggling?

turns.speaker: Aditi Sriram
turns.text: Giving regions that power might start a competition to keep cutting taxes, especially when the areas are relatively small. Letting them target particular discounts might make more sense. Central government could also provide an investment fund that lets places with less tax income borrow for infrastructure.

evidence.quote: regions that are not able to borrow as much through their retained taxes can still borrow from that fund, invest into infrastructure, and build the capacity to invest into infrastructure.
we might see a race to the bottom if we devolve taxes. Regions are just far too small.
There might be reason to devolve the ability to target reliefs, because rates relief for certain sectors in different areas might look different.

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: Local councils could set rates before 1990. There were worries then about councils raising a tax paid by businesses rather than voters. Giving areas more power now could also produce competition to cut rates. Either way, it's harder to judge the results while people mistake who ultimately bears the cost.

evidence.quote: Before 1990, rates multipliers were set locally. That was changed by a Conservative Government, because they thought that there was a problem if the people paying the tax were not the people who were voting.
There are also potential problems the other way in terms of tax competition
the person who, in the long term, bears the economic incidence, so the landlord.

chapters.title: Should online sales be taxed?
chapters.takeaway: Aditi Sriram proposed taxing larger online sellers, while Dan Neidle argued that the tax would add complexity without correcting the problem she identified.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: As more shopping moves online, should the government tax online sales differently?

evidence.quote: There have been calls to look at how online sales should be taxed. It would be good to hear from all of you about what the Government should be looking at in this space

turns.speaker: Aditi Sriram
turns.text: Our tax system hasn't kept up with retail. Online sellers can make substantial sales from warehouses rather than expensive high street premises; 28% of sales were online in September 2026. We propose a 2% tax on online sales, with a 1% rate for click and collect, exceptions for essentials and a threshold so smaller businesses wouldn't pay it.

evidence.quote: Online retail is the best example of that because it can operate out of warehouses that do not occupy space on expensive high streets and are able to generate so much more turnover.
In September 2026, 28% of sales happened online
What we have proposed is a 2% tax on online sales.
we can have a reduced 1% rate on click and collect
We can exempt essentials in line with VAT. We can also protect small businesses by having a small business threshold of £500,000

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: I don't accept that business rates put physical shops at the tax disadvantage this proposal assumes: over time, landlords largely bear them. An online sales tax would mean defining which sales count, making exceptions and imposing new paperwork across the economy, for what I think would be relatively little revenue.

evidence.quote: Tenants pay business rates, but, over time, it is the landlords bearing the rates. There is not a problem to solve with an online sales tax.
You then have to exempt business-to-business sales. Even people who mainly sell to businesses would have to comply with an online sales tax.

You have to decide what is and what is not online, and what is and what is not click and collect, with a significant degree of complexity across the whole economy, and for what? For peanuts—a couple of billion.

turns.speaker: Chris Curtis
turns.text: Even apart from tax, doesn't a physical shop cost more to run while giving people a useful place to see a product before they buy it—possibly online? Shouldn't policy recognise that benefit?

evidence.quote: there is a cost of having a physical business over an online one.
you are also providing a service to people, the ability to go and look at a thing, which is not captured in a sale if people later go and buy it online.
Are those positive externalities not something that, in principle, we should capture in the tax system?

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: Online shopping benefits people too, including those who live far from large stores or can't easily leave home. We should be careful about using a tax to push people away from a way of shopping they choose.

evidence.quote: There are also lots of positive benefits from online sales. People choose it because it is convenient. They choose it because they live away from large stores. They choose it because they cannot get out of the house so easily. We should be very careful about trying to override people’s preferences, which is what an online sales tax would do.
